title: A rain cloud at the navel
hook: a rainbow poster says yellow; the old text says the color of a rain cloud
carry: dhyana: hold the form as the tradition gives it
tomorrow: the top of the map isn't the end of the trip. where does she go next?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the map's lines: Ida with the moon, Pingala with the sun, and Ekalavya before his clay teacher: some practices are handed on, guru to student. Today, its colors.
screen: `ONE MAP, TWO WAYS TO HAND IT ON.`

segments.voice: On a yoga studio wall there's a poster: circles stacked up a seated figure, red at the base, yellow at the navel, on up to violet at the crown. A neat rainbow. Now open the Sat-Cakra-Nirupana, an old Sanskrit text on these centers, to the lotus at the navel. It isn't yellow. The text says it's the color of a heavy rain cloud: dark, full, about to break.
screen: `A RAINBOW ON THE STUDIO WALL.` → `YELLOW AT THE NAVEL.` → `THE OLD TEXT: A RAIN CLOUD.`

segments.voice: The text calls this lotus Manipura, and inside the rain cloud it sets a region of fire, a seed sound, ram, and a deity seated there. Every lotus gets a picture like that, detail by detail. Why so exact? Hindus tell a story about that. A five-year-old prince, Dhruva, was turned away from his father's lap by his stepmother, and he left for the forest, hurt and set on finding God. The sage Narada met him on the way, gave him a mantra, and then did something careful: he described Vishnu's form for the boy to hold, the gentle smiling face, the four arms with conch, discus, mace and lotus. Dhruva held that picture so steadily that one day it vanished from his heart, he opened his eyes, and Vishnu stood before him in that very form. That's dhyana, meditation on a form, and it's one of the most ordinary things in Hindu worship. Many pujas open with a dhyana verse that paints the deity, the color, the hands, what each hand holds, so the worshipper sees clearly before offering anything. The details aren't decoration. Holding them is the practice. So the rain cloud matters, not because anyone's navel is gray, but because it's the form a meditator is given. Now the poster. Its rainbow is tidy and may help a beginner remember an order, but scholars trace it to much later, largely Western books, not to this text. So the honest move is to name which map you're using, and when you sit with the old one, hold it as it was given, the way Narada gave Vishnu to Dhruva: rain cloud and all.
screen: `MANIPURA: A RAIN CLOUD, FIRE, AND RAM.` · `NARADA GIVES DHRUVA A FORM TO HOLD.` · `DHYANA: MEDITATION ON A FORM.` · `THE DETAILS ARE THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `RAIN CLOUD AND ALL.`

segments.voice: Choose a form to hold: a deity you love, as you've seen it in a home shrine or a temple, or simply the dark rain cloud of today's lotus. Close your eyes and build it detail by detail: the color first, then the shape, then one small thing in it. When it blurs, start again with the color.
The chakras as a map: at the navel, Manipura, the color of a heavy rain cloud in the old text, not the yellow of the poster.
screen: `THE CHAKRAS AS A MAP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to this: dhyana, holding the form as the tradition gives it. Rain cloud and all. That's day sixteen forty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1649 COUNTS.` → `THE TANTRAS, FRAMED · 41 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: THE TOP ISN'T THE END. WHERE NEXT?`

howItsDone: Many pujas begin with a dhyana verse describing the deity's form so the worshipper can picture it; in tantric chakra meditation, practitioners likewise picture each lotus with the colors, letters and seed sounds their text gives. Popular rainbow charts are a later, simpler scheme seen in some classes.

Sat-Cakra-Nirupana.meaning: a Sanskrit text describing the centers along the spine

Ida.meaning: the left channel, linked with the moon

Pingala.meaning: the right channel, linked with the sun

dhyana.meaning: meditation; here, holding a form in the mind

Dhruva.meaning: a boy prince whose meditation on Vishnu is told in the Bhagavata Purana

Narada.meaning: a wandering sage and devotee of Vishnu

sources.ref: Sat-Cakra-Nirupana (the Manipura lotus at the navel, the color of a heavy rain cloud, with the region of fire, the seed syllable ram and its deity; each lotus given its own colors, lettered petals, central shape and seed syllable)

Bhagavata Purana 4.8–4.9 (Dhruva, turned away from his father's lap by his stepmother Suruchi, goes to the forest; Narada gives him a mantra and describes Vishnu's form to meditate on; when the form vanishes from his heart he opens his eyes and sees Vishnu in that form)
Dhyana verses recited at the start of puja (describing the deity's form for the worshipper to picture)
Kurt Leland, Rainbow Body: A History of the Western Chakra System from Blavatsky to Brennan (2016): the rainbow color scheme as a later Western development
